translations.text: The Ascetic Work of Abba Ephraim. Bless us. 99.
Suffering compels me to speak, while my unworthiness rebukes me and tells me to remain silent.
Again, the pains of my heart torment me into speaking, while my sins reproach me and tell me to stop.
Since I am caught between the two, it is better for me to speak than to remain silent.
I will speak so that I may find relief from the pains of my heart. My soul is distressed within me, and my eyes shed tears.
Oh, who will put water upon my head and a fountain of tears upon my eyes, so that I may weep
day and night over the wounds of my soul, because the word of instruction has ceased to be effective in our times, and because we are ignorant, for our sins have multiplied?
For pride does not let us recognize what has come upon us, so that we might stop sinning.
The instruction and teaching of our fathers used to shine like the lights of heaven, because they practiced every kind of good conduct,
especially since they were surrounded by thorns and thistles—I mean the pagans and heretics who lived in their times.
But they were precious, like genuine stones of great value.
Moreover, because of their truthful words and their way of life, their enemies and those who hated them were jealous of them.
For who would see their humility and not be moved?
Or who would see them in their gentleness and tranquility and not marvel?
Who would see their contempt for money and not hate the world?
What greedy or proud person would see the dignity of their lives and not turn to what is right?
What sexually immoral or impure person has ever seen them standing in prayer
without becoming worthy and pure? What angry or impatient person would meet them and not immediately turn to gentleness?
They struggled here and were given joy in the place of eternal celebrations.
God was glorified through them, and many people were built up through them.
But our instruction has stopped traveling along straight roads and has traveled along difficult and wearisome roads.
For nowadays no one leaves his possessions behind for God's sake.
And no one renounces them for the sake of eternal life. Nowadays no one is gentle, nor is anyone humble.
Nowadays no one bears being insulted.
Nor does anyone bear being ridiculed.
For we have all become senseless.
We have all become irritable, hot-tempered, and envious.
We have all become arrogant.
We have sought fine, beautifully made clothes, being boastful, loving empty glory, and loving our own comfort.
For someone who comes in to join the brothers, to the place where he is to be settled, wants to lead others.
He wants to teach before he has been taught anything at all.
He wants to lay down the law before he has learned anything at all about the law.
He wants to be a philosopher before he has learned a syllable.
He wants others to submit to him before he has learned to submit.
He wants to give orders before he has learned to take orders.
The one who is advanced in age gives orders with authority.
But the young boy talks back and argues.
If a rich man comes in to join the brothers, he demands greater honor from us.
If a poor man comes in, he seeks comfort that he has not known.
If he was a laborer in the world, he pampers his body so that it becomes smooth, and his fingers so that they become soft.
My dear brothers, who would not weep [?] when he sees our way of life bearing no fruit?
Those who have renounced the world are once again thinking about worldly things.
And those who say, “We have renounced earthly things,” desire them all the more.
Those who say of themselves, “We are spiritual,” make even more use of earthly things.
They think about things of the flesh in the thoughts of their hearts. We do not know, brothers, the task to which we have been called.
We do not know, my dear ones, the honor into which we have entered.
We were called to self-control, yet we seek varied meals.
We came in to embrace nakedness, yet we worry about fine, beautifully made clothes.
We came in to suffer with our Lord, yet we seek our own comfort in everything.
We came in to submit.
And we all persist in disobedience, though we were called to wisdom, understanding, and knowledge.
And we are savage toward one another.
We read, but we do not understand what we read.
We listen, but the words do not enter the ears of our hearts.
If someone encounters a murderer on the road, his face changes and his heart is troubled.
We too see and hear the words of the apostles who were killed and the prophets who were sawn apart and stoned. Instead of weeping and groaning,
we laugh and joke, and we feel nothing at all.
Every day we hear that the Word of God was persecuted.
They mocked him and flogged him. They hung him on a tree and crucified him. They pierced him and killed him, and he died because of our sins.
Even at these things we are not afraid, but our hearts go astray.
And we are careless, laughing amid our cares.
The sun could not bear to see its Lord being mocked. It grieved and turned its light into darkness.
But we are unwilling to turn our hearts from darkness to light.
The curtain of his temple, which had committed no sin, split down the middle.
But we are unwilling to stir our hearts and weep over our own sins.
The earth often shakes beneath us and trembles before the face of the Lord. But we are not afraid, though we are disobedient to the Lord.
The earth opened and swallowed cities, closing over them because of God's wrath. Even so, we were not afraid.
The sun was eclipsed many times and became dark in the middle of the day. Darkness covered us at noon.
Even so, we were not afraid. Our hearts felt nothing, nor were we troubled. The wars of the Persians and the other barbarians—
they killed people, ravaged the regions, and laid the land waste.
They poured out much blood, so that we might see, become afraid, and run to God with weeping and repentance. Even after these things, we did not turn away from our evil ways.
Brothers, let us repent, lest God's wrath come upon us.
Brothers, let us bow down and weep, so that we may avert God's wrath and he may forgive us, for we have provoked him.
Brothers, let us humble our souls with fasting, hardships, and nights of keeping watch. Let us walk in truth, so that he may have mercy on us and fill the earth with joy.
Let us mourn, so that the Holy Spirit may console us and comfort us.
Let us throw off our evil habits.
Let us clothe ourselves in good virtues, especially we who have been counted worthy of the angelic way of life.
Let us establish a good standard and rule for ourselves.
Let us strive to imitate the lives of our early fathers, persevering patiently.
Let us not practice self-control today and abandon it tomorrow.
Let us not walk barefoot today and then tomorrow look for fine sandals to wear.
Let us not wear a tunic or sackcloth today and then tomorrow look for a fine, splendid robe.
Do not conduct yourself with understanding today and then live without restraint tomorrow.
Do not live in obedience today and then become disobedient tomorrow, raging harshly or shouting.
Do not conduct yourself humbly and gently today, and then with arrogance and pride tomorrow.
Do not weep or mourn over your sins today and then let yourself go tomorrow, living in merriment and empty laughter.
Do not sleep on the ground today and then sleep on high beds tomorrow.
But I urge you, my brothers, to establish for yourselves a standard and a fixed rule, with patience and perseverance, so that you may be able to complete your lives in a way pleasing to God.
Let each of you help your neighbor in everything. Discipline your bodies through ascetic practices, and please your fathers and your brothers in accordance with God.
Listen to the Lord saying, “Just as you want people to do to you, you yourselves should also do to them.”
Therefore, my beloved, persevere in your good work, remaining steadfast and not allowing yourself to be turned aside.
For our fathers attained perfection, persevering in a single rule, and patiently completed the work they had begun.
Some spent forty or fifty years without changing their good practice of self-control.
They abstained from varied foods, controlled their tongues, slept on the ground, and lived in humility, gentleness, faith, love, and unity of heart.
They loved their neighbors, which is the bond of spiritual perfection.
Besides all this, they acquired nothing for themselves on earth, keeping free from the cares of this life.
They devoted themselves entirely to prayer and their nightly vigils, with weeping and sighing.
Their bodies served them only for necessities, and they trampled pride underfoot.
They renounced anger, and gold and silver were foreign to them. Through their hardships and sufferings, they purified themselves from every evil deed.
Therefore God dwelt in them and was glorified in them. Everyone who meets them, and those who hear about them, benefit from them and glorify God.
Let us too strive to be like them and leave behind every evil deed that God hates, so that we may be purified and God may dwell within us too and save us from the evil one.
Tell me about this matter frankly.
If someone throws you down into a pit of filth and leaves you there, will you put up with him?
If you, then, who are a worm, cannot bear this, how will God—the undefiled, the spotless, the holy—dwell within you while you remain in the filth of defilement and stench?
Let us therefore purify ourselves, my dear friends, so that God may dwell within us and we may share in his promises.
Do not dishonor his holy name, which has been pronounced over us, since we have been named after Christ and called Christians.
Let us walk in truth, for Christ is the truth, so that the Holy Spirit may dwell within us.
For where Christ dwells, there is freedom.
Let us be sober-minded so that we may understand that he has invited us to his wedding.
Let us love him as he loved us. Let us strive in everything so that we may be worthy of his wedding hall.
Do not let us be careless, lest they find our clothing filthy, bind us, and throw us out of the wedding hall.
And they will condemn us on two counts, because we have indeed left the world, yet we think about the things of the world.
We flee from fleshly things, yet once again we seek their comforts.
Do not do this, then, my dear friends. Instead, remember that the day of the Lord is coming like a thief.
Let us be afraid that that day may come upon us suddenly, and we may be found naked and become wretched.
For it will come in an instant, before we realize it and take notice. For, as he said, in the days of Noah they were eating and drinking,
taking wives and living with husbands, and they did not realize it until the flood came and destroyed them all.
Let us therefore be afraid, my dear friends, and be ready, lest they come upon me while we are not ready and no help is available to us.
The day has drawn near. What is written has been fulfilled; these things have finished taking place, and nothing remains except the deeds of the Antichrist.
For his wickedness must reach its full extent when the kingdom of the Romans comes to an end.
Already the one who is coming is on his way, and he will not delay.
Whoever wants to reign with Christ the King must not neglect himself, for the time has drawn near, according to what is written in Revelation.
Therefore, whoever wants to escape the fire of Gehenna and the worm that never sleeps must strive well.
Let him be afraid and remain watchful.
Whoever wants to be comforted must mourn now.
Whoever wants to be exalted in the kingdom of heaven must humble himself here and now.
Whoever wants to rejoice with the angels must weep here and now.
Be sober. Keep your lamp shining. Keep oil in your vessels.
Keep your clothing shining.
Stay watchful.
Do not sleep, for the hour
has drawn near, along with the bridal chamber, which is filled with joy and gladness forever.
For the king’s city, the true bridal chamber, which is filled with every good thing, is the heavenly Jerusalem.
It is light, with no darkness in it. It is a spring filled with living water.
Whoever wants to live in it with Christ the King must hurry and prepare himself.
For the time has grown short, and the day is drawing to a close. No one knows what will happen to him.
Let us not sleep, lest he shut the door on us and say, “I do not know you.”
Otherwise, a cloud of darkness will come upon us, with a storm, winds, thunder, lightning, and troubles on every side, and we will have no opportunity to go anywhere.
My brothers, let us repent. Let us not come under God’s judgment.
Listen to the writer of Proverbs saying, “When trouble comes upon you and disaster overtakes you, you will cry out to me.
But I will not listen to you, because I called to you and you did not listen to me.
And I spread my words before you, but you paid no attention.”
So let us obey the Lord.
Let us realize that we are in a foreign land.
Let us hurry to go to our city.
But we, brothers, are spiritual merchants. Let us acquire for ourselves the pearl, Christ Jesus.
Woe to anyone who does not acquire him for himself! Such a person has handed himself over to destruction.
Or do you not know, brothers, that we are branches of the true vine, Christ, and that Christ’s Father is the gardener?
So take care, brothers, that none of you remains fruitless.
But understand that the Father is the one who tends the vine. He prunes those that bear fruit so that they may bear more fruit.
Those that do not bear fruit he throws out of the vine to burn them in a fire.
Let us therefore watch ourselves, brothers, lest we become careless and bear no fruit.
Then we will be cut off from the vine, become strangers to Christ, and be thrown into Gehenna and the unquenchable fire.
But we, brothers, are good seed, which Christ, the Lord of the earth, has sown in his field.
Let us therefore understand and recognize that the harvest has drawn near. The reapers have prepared the sickles and are waiting for God's command.
Take care, then: do not let him find weeds among us, so that we are bound into bundles to be burned.
Or do you not know, brothers, that we are destined to cross a terrifying sea?
For this reason I am afraid that a wind may suddenly blow, and they may find us unprepared, bind our arms, wrap us up, and take us to the threshing floor of judgment.
Then we will find no defense and will weep in that place over our negligence, while we see others rejoicing, exulting, and celebrating.
We ourselves, meanwhile, will be dragged to Hades in affliction, in hardships upon hardships, and in anguish,
with bitter groans because of our negligence and laziness, because we did not prepare ourselves before they came for us.
No, then, brothers, let us not be careless, because God's judgment is terrifying.
Do not let the passions of the flesh make us strangers to the city of Christ, so that we are thrown out of the wedding chamber and fall down into the place of weeping and gnashing of teeth.
Instead, brothers, let us be sober and recognize that we have taken the monastic habit.
Let us not find ourselves under the rule of the passions of the flesh,
among them in quarrels and joking, in excessive, pointless laughter. These things reveal that we are stripped of God's glory.
Gluttony and worldly pride reveal that we seek defilement.
Love of money and arrogance reveal that we do not love God.
Envy and fiery anger tell us that God's love is not within us.
Flesh that is fat and sleek from excessive washing and anointing reveals that we love the passions and are slaves to defilement.
Our mouths are open, and we never keep silent. Whatever words we wish to say, whether good or bad, we pour them out without restraint.
We have paid no attention to what is written: “When you speak many words, you will not escape sin.”
As long as we remain in things like these, it is all in vain: the habit will not benefit us.
Instead, we are merely making fools of ourselves while our hearts are occupied with such things.
Monk, do not trust in the habit. Instead, recognize that you are a stranger to the things of heaven, and that your soul is plainly naked.
Perhaps, then, someone will say, “The passions of the body are natural, and there is no blame for anyone who serves them.”
So take care, brother, not to bring an accusation against yourself
by turning the creatures of the good God toward things contrary to nature because of your desires and your negligence.
For everything God created is very good.
He adorned their nature with beauties, with functions suitable for human beings, and with good activities.
That is, someone may be hungry naturally; there is no fault in him if he eats in moderation.
But if he eats greedily, he will be guilty of wrongdoing.
For [?] is natural.
Likewise, someone may be thirsty; there is no fault in him if he drinks in moderation.
But if he drinks insatiably, he is found at fault, because this too is something natural.
Insatiability, however, is contrary to nature.
If someone sleeps as nature requires, there is no fault in him.

But if he sleeps beyond measure, he gains no honor from it, because he has relaxed his body excessively, giving it over to the passion for sleep and surrendering himself to fantasies through negligence.
If the habit of sleeping becomes excessive, it masters what is natural.
For nature and habit are the heralds of the two sides.
Nature reveals itself as a slave, while habit reveals the will. For a person stands between the two sides.
The will, however, is its own master.
It is like a farmer who plants bad habits and good virtues in nature. According to his wishes, he plants what is bad
in this way: in hunger, gluttony;
in thirst, greed;
and in sleep, excessive relaxation through prolonged sleep.
Again, in the sight of the eyes, evil thoughts; in habitual practice, lying.
He also plants the good virtues in this same way:
in thirst, endurance;
in sleep, a night of keeping watch;
in lying, [?] the truth;
in the sight of the eyes, decency.
For the will is like the farmer.
For in the blink of an eye he uproots bad habits and plants good virtues as he wishes, since he has gained mastery over nature.
For nature is like a field that is cultivated.
Its farmer is free choice.
Holy Scripture therefore teaches us and shows us which bad habits deserve to be pulled out by their roots,
and which good virtues ought to be planted and cultivated, while the farmer remains watchful.
For the farmer who does not know the power of the Scriptures is powerless and unskilled.
For the instruction of the Scriptures gives strength and wisdom, and supplies good virtues from its own branches in this way:
It gives him good faith to plant in his unbelief, and hope amid distrust,
and love amid hatred, knowledge amid ignorance, diligence amid carelessness, and honor and glory.
The one who labors plants immortality, and divinity within his humanity.
So if our farmer—that is, free choice—abandons his teacher, who instructs him—that is, Holy Scripture—he is found wandering astray,
and he falls into evil thoughts, with evil [?] gathering within him, planting them in his nature, although they did not belong to it.
These are unbelief and giving up on yourself,
hatred, envy, love of empty glory, anger of heart, quarrelsomeness, talking back, contention, and things like these.
These things have come upon him because he abandoned the lawgiver.
But if he comes to his senses and finds fault with himself, hurries to bow before the lawgiver, and says with tears, “I have sinned, for I abandoned you,”
immediately the lawgiver takes the initiative toward him in his great love for humanity,
and gives him good wisdom and strength to cultivate the field of nature again,
so that he may uproot the bad habits from it. He gives him excellent and good virtues to plant in place of the bad ones, and gives him crowns and many honors.
He became hungry by nature, but he endured.
He felt desire, but he became dry.
Sleep weighed heavily on him, but he struggled to keep watch through the night.
He is reluctant to sing psalms.
But he opens his mouth and blesses God with determined effort.
Such a person is therefore crowned and honored.
The crowns are because he struggled and overcame nature.
The honors are because he has acquired the good virtues for himself.
So let us now glorify God’s love for humanity, and let us bless him and proclaim his goodness.
Let us bow down and worship his compassion.
For what father would show compassion like this?
Or what father loves his children as the Lord loves us, his servants?
He has freely given us great gifts, caring for us generously.
He forgives us mercifully and compassionately heals the wounds of the soul.
But we, ungrateful as we are, will reject him.
He is patient with us and does not abandon us. For he wants everyone to be saved and to stop sinning, to stop sinning, so that they may inherit his kingdom.
For in his goodness he has provided a remedy for all our painful and severe illnesses.
He makes the lazy person diligent, rousing him to hymns and psalms.
He urges the sinner to repent, forgives him, and gives him courage to pursue virtue with tears and humility.
He listens quickly to the weak person so that he will not lose heart, and he freely gives the gift of the Spirit to those who persevere.
He honors them all as a reward for their labor.
He has the power to draw us to himself by force, but he does not want our free choice to be fruitless.
O good God!
O God who loves humanity!
O God beyond description!
Yet we treat him with contempt and neglect to seek him, although he is our Lord. He is the one who created us, and because he loved us, he gave himself for us. Yet we are too lazy to call on him.
He redeemed us.
He helped us.
He enlightened the eyes of our mind.
He gave knowledge to our heart.
He made us taste the sweetness of his love, which is delightful at all times.
Blessed, then, is the one who will be filled with his love, for no other desire rules over him.
Listen, then, my beloved brothers.
What wise person would not love such a Lord?
Who would not worship him and give him praise?
I beg and urge you not to neglect to praise this gentle Lord.
If we are negligent, then, you who love God, what defense will we have on the day of judgment? Or what will we say?
Will we say, “We did not hear,” or “We did not understand,” or “No one told us”?
Woe, woe! [?] upon us!
He said, “Voices were heard in the valley of judgment.”
What, then, are these voices, my brothers, except weeping and gnashing of teeth?
What has our Lord, who is in his Father’s embrace, not done for us?
He who is in the indescribable heights—did he not humble himself and come down to us?
He who is invisible—was he not seen for your sake?
The immortal Word took on flesh and tasted death for us.
He who gives honor to everyone—was he not dishonored?
Did they not strike him in the face for your sake, so that he might set them free?
Oh, this awe-inspiring wonder!
A hand of clay, a hand of earth and ashes, formed from the earth, dared to strike the face of Christ, who formed heaven and earth! And he endured it humbly.
Yet we, miserable, wretched people, who are earth and ashes, cannot even bear one another’s words.
Did not the immortal one taste death and undergo burial for your sake, so that he might raise us up?
Did he not undo the enemy’s bonds, bind him, and hand him over to us to mock him, giving us authority to trample on him?
On what day did we cry out to him without his listening to us?
Even if we have to wait a little, he wants our reward to increase.
Listen, beloved brother, as I speak to you.
Monk, tell me: why did you renounce the world if you are going to seek the world’s comforts again? Will you not answer me? Will you not come to your senses?
Do you not know that you were called to afflictions and hardships, to hunger and thirst, to cold and nakedness?
You were called, beloved, to prayers, nights of vigilance, tears, and sighs.
Yet you, brother, go about in frivolity, indulgence, and laughter. You do not restrain your mouth or your eyes, and you do not guard your heart.
Remember, then, that you were called to a heavenly inheritance, yet you act foolishly in forgetfulness, thinking about earthly things.
What will you say on the day of judgment?
Will not the true judge say to you, “Did I not suffer for your sake?
I went hungry for your sake. I was thirsty, and they gave me vinegar to drink.
I was naked on the cross.
I gave my life for you.”
Are these words not written for you, brother?
Or do you not know that all creation will be made to stand before the judgment seat of Christ, and everyone will be judged for every deed they have forgotten, whether good or evil?
We will be rebuked amid thousands upon thousands and tens of thousands upon tens of thousands of angels and archangels and all the saints, standing around him.
Will you be able to lie at that time?
Watch out, then, monk. Do not let your condemnation be doubled against you and find yourself disgraced because of your evil deeds.
But I beg you: rise from your slumber, leave your forgetfulness behind, and prepare yourself before God’s judgment.
Realize that it has drawn near: the day is waning, and the hour has drawn near.
Take notice and see: our brothers were with us yesterday, but today they are no longer here.
For their Lord called for them, and they departed.
Consider yesterday and today: it has passed like a flower of the grass or like a runner hurrying along.
This is how our days will pass without our noticing.
Blessed is the one who prepares himself, for he will receive everlasting life.
Listen to me, beloved.
How long will you remain careless? How long will you be caught up in material concerns, when this life is like a place of [?]?
Pay attention now and recognize what you have sent up to heaven ahead of you.
I beg you: do not go empty-handed, but send a gift ahead of you.
Send a prayer full of tears.
Send gifts of charity from the labor of your hands.
Send nights of watching, with psalms and hymns.
Send faith and love toward God, who loved you.
If you have sent these things ahead of you in this way, then take courage, because you will go to a place of rest forever.
But if you have sent nothing ahead of you from among the things I have spoken of,
at least do not offend your neighbor. Do not act arrogantly toward him.
And why do you worry excessively about a tunic, a cloak, and food?
Brother, you swear oaths, lie, and cheat in your receiving and giving.
Will the one who feeds the birds and the animals not also feed you through his providence and the fruit of your hands?
Do not act this way, monk, but look forward to becoming an heir of God.
And yet you worry about the material things of this age!
In keeping with your monastic habit, you say, “I have died to the world.” Yet again you think about worldly things.
Why do you deceive yourself?
Why do you enslave yourself?
The time for repentance lies before you, yet you are negligent and find fault with the lawgiver.
Take heed, then, you wretched man: death will come suddenly. And what will you say?
Will you be able to say, “Leave me! Do not take me now! Leave me until I repent”?
Be alert, you wretched man, because that hour is coming upon you like a snare. You will regret it and say, “Oh, woe to me! My days have vanished, and I did not notice!”
Woe to me!
What am I going to do?
Death has surrounded me; there is no way to escape in any direction.
Now, then, my beloved, be alert and pay attention to what I am saying.
Listen to what the Lord says.
He said, “Even for a single idle word, a person will give an account on the day of judgment.”
This is enough to fill us with fear and trembling at the day of Christ’s judgment.
Who, then, would not be astonished that the Lord of all is calling out, yet there is no one who listens to him?
He said, “The wedding hall is ready. My oxen and fattened animals have been slaughtered. Everything is ready.
Come to the wedding!
Come! Look, the door is open!
Come! Do not stay outside; otherwise…
If I shut the door, there is no one who will open it for you. Whoever remains outside will have no one to bring him in.
And after these calls, after all these pleas, no one listens, no one hurries, no one is afraid. Instead, our hearts have been bound by empty deception, and we do not want to listen.
Let us be sober.
Do not let us be careless and be swept away for nothing.
Blessed is the person who has run eagerly and gone to the Lord, for he will have confidence in the true bridal chamber.
Oh, woe to the one who has been careless!
We know that we must depart, and we know that he is coming with power and immense glory, to place crowns on those who obeyed him and worked well, and to rebuke those who were careless.
For just as, in the middle of the night, when all humanity is oblivious and sunk in a deep sleep, a loud noise comes from heaven, with peals of thunder
that inspire terror, flashes of lightning full of fire, and mighty winds full of fury, and those who are sleeping wake up trembling and are seized by fear,
and are suddenly terrified, and each one remembers his own deeds, whether evil or good,
those who have done evil will lament and beat their chests, weeping and crying out, “Woe to us! Where shall we go?”
For the earth will shake and give way beneath them. The thunder will terrify them, the fiery lightning will make them tremble, and the winds will strike them and shake them.
Dense gloom and darkness will bewilder them, and there will be no way to flee in any direction.
The fear of death oppresses them. The memory of their sins surrounds them. The rebuke of judgment convicts them.
This is how that hour will come.
A terrifying trumpet will sound in heaven, awakening with its terror those who sleep in the depths of the earth, those who have died since the beginning of time, and making them rise.
Then the powers of heaven will shake, and the foundations of the earth will heave, roaring like the sea. All its elements will tremble in fear of the Lord’s glory.
For a terrifying fire will go before him, cleansing the earth of the lawless deeds with which they defiled it. [?]
Hades will open its gates in fear. Death will retreat and cease to exist.
Then all human flesh that came from the earth, all those who have crumbled away, will hear the sound of the trumpet and will all come to life.
Oh, this terrifying wonder! How, in the blink of an eye,
the bones of all humanity will rise and come to life, and they will stand for judgment, crying out in fear and saying, “Glory to you, God, who raised us because of his love for humanity!”
Oh, blessed are the perfect and those who have practiced self-discipline in purity, for they will rejoice when they see the reward for their toil.
And the martyrs will wear their crowns, and the prophets and apostles will adorn themselves, and they will all be in glory before the face of Christ.
Oh, blessed are those who will be found worthy of that coming, for they will meet the angels as they walk with the saints.
to meet the Lord in the air, on the clouds of glory, and celebrate with the immortal bridegroom.
For just as a bird trusts its wings and flies up high on them,
so each person sees according to their own condition.
The person whose heart is pure sees the glory of God.
Adam, the first human being, will marvel on that day and say, “How did these vast multitudes and these countless nations come from me?”
But he will be even more bewildered: “How is it that, from this one creation of all humanity, some are in the kingdom and others are in Hades?”
Glory to you, God, who alone are wise!
So then, brothers, let us remember that terrifying place of judgment.
Indeed, when I remembered it, trembling seized me. I was shaken, I sighed, and I wept as I saw the paradise of delight and the pit of Gehenna of [?] before Christ’s judgment seat.
When I saw this, I sighed. My strength failed because I had spent my time in negligence and empty thoughts.
These are the things on which I wasted my tears, and I did not notice how they passed away, how my days passed away.
My days came to an end without my realizing it. My sins multiplied.
Woe to me, my beloved!
What will I do about the shame that will seize me on that terrifying day of true judgment,
when those who know me will look at me?

I wear the monastic habit, and they look at me and call us blessed. They do not know that my inner self is full of lawlessness and every kind of impurity, for I have forgotten God, who examines hearts and kidneys.
Truly, brothers, the shame at that time is great. Above all, it is a great love that cannot be dissolved.
Truly, miserable is the person who will be thrown out in shame on that day.
Who, then, will help him?
I implore you by your mercies, O God who loves humanity and is good: do not place me at your left. Do not cast me out with the goats who have provoked you, and do not say, “I do not know you.”

Instead, because of your abundant mercy, give me the opportunity, as long as I am in the body, to keep weeping day and night, sighing over my sins, so that you may prepare my heart as a dwelling place for holy grace.
Even though I am an ungodly sinner, I will not stop knocking at the door of your mercy.
Even though I am negligent, I will not give up on your path, my God.
I beg you, my brothers.
I beg you.
I appeal to you.
Let us weep before him night and day, with prayers, blessings, and psalms,
so that we do not fall into the place of weeping and gnashing of teeth, of the sleepless worm, of shame and reproach, and of the great judgment that cuts off. Perhaps
through God's mercies he will make us worthy of eternal life with the saints, in the place where there is neither fear nor destruction,
the place where there is no death,
the place where there is no warfare by the adversary,
the place where there is neither hatred nor hostility, but lasting joy and gladness, and a table filled with every spiritual good thing,
and filled with the sweetness of righteousness. And we will ascend to paradise, for we will inherit it forever and ever.
Glory and majesty to God, who is good and loves humanity, who has prepared his kingdom for us forever and ever. Amen.
Again, Apa Ephraim himself, writing to a beloved disciple of his who was receiving instruction from him.
My beloved in the Lord, first of all, in everything, put humility in your mouth, being ready to answer, “Forgive me,” knowing that through humility all the enemy's power is shattered.
And you know the goodness of your Master, and what was said about him:
“He became humble and obedient to the point of death.”
You too, my son, put humility in your mouth, your heart, and your neck. For when you come to humility, it has its own commandments.
Look at David boasting of humility.
He spoke these words: “I humbled myself, and the Lord saved me and did good to me.”
You too, my son, clothe yourself in humility, so that God's virtues may be with you.
If, my son, you remain in humility, no passion will be able to come near you.
A humble person—there is no measure to his beauty.
A humble person—no passion will be able to come near you.
A humble person—there is no measure to his beauty.
A humble person is a sacrifice to God.
A humble person puts the heart of God and his angels at ease.
Moreover, the angels honor him.
There is cause for reproach in someone who has acquired every virtue whatsoever.
But as for someone who has acquired humility for himself, you find no cause for reproach in him at all, because he has become humble.
These are the virtues of a humble person, my son.
Be silent, my son, for it is written, “The wise person will keep silent at that time.”
You too, be silent until you are asked.
If you are asked a question, speak gently and humbly.
Do not be sullen at all.
If someone is older than you, sit down.
Do not speak if harmful words are spoken. Lie down and put the thought out of your mind, saying, “I have not heard a single word.” This too is beneficial.
Be all the more obedient to them.
For it is written, “Be doers of the word, and not merely hearers; otherwise you deceive yourself,” my son in the Lord.
I entrust their commandments to you at the beginning.
You too must keep them in your youth.
Look at what Paul says.
He also said, “From your childhood you have known the holy writings, which can save you.”
You too must learn the whole order of monastic life,
so that you may be worthy of love in all your deeds.
If you go to a mountain to settle there while you are young,
attach yourself to someone older than you who has God within him. Do not leave him in your recklessness and go to someone else.
Let the person to whom you attach yourself test you, so that you do not make him angry.
For it is written, “Is it a small thing for you to provoke people to anger?”
On the mountain where you are, observe this rule: do not run from place to place.
Do not call on people for your own comfort and to satisfy your appetite.
Do not make friends with troublemakers,
so that you may remain at peace and not be talked about by the brothers.
I beg you, my beloved in the Lord: this is your beginning. Learn to listen, so that you may find rest.
For it is written, “Gain instruction, not silver.”
Guard yourself against disobedience, so that the saying about Saul and the rebuke he received may not be fulfilled in you.
For God is won over by obedience more than by sacrifice.
These, then, are the rules of monastic life.
When you eat with brothers,
Do not raise your head until you have finished eating.
Eat from the dish you reach toward.
If you lack anything at the table, do not say, “Bring it,” while someone older than you is sitting there.
If you want to drink from the cup, do not let your throat make a loud noise like worldly people do.
If you are sitting among the brothers and phlegm comes into your mouth, do not spit it out among them.
Go some distance away and spit it out.
When you sleep in a place with brothers, do not lie within a cubit of them.
If possible, do not sleep two together on a mat when you are a young boy.
Do not sleep naked or on your back, so that dreams do not disturb you.
When you walk with brothers, keep some distance from them so that you can pay attention to your heart.
If you walk with a brother and have sandals on your feet, but the person walking with you has none, take yours off too and walk as he does.
For it is written, “Endure hardship.”
Do the work; do not announce it.
Be diligent while you are in your dwelling.
Do not eat while the sun is up.
Do not cook for yourself alone and indulge yourself.
But if you are told to cook for yourself, invite a poor person who is on the mountain with you, so that you too can boast, “I have not eaten my bread alone.”
If you are on a mountain or in a place where a brother is sick, visit him twice each day: in the morning before you begin your manual work, and in the evening.
For it is written, my beloved in the Lord, “I was sick, and you visited me.”
If a brother dies on the mountain where you are, do not remain in your cell. As soon as you hear, go and sit beside him and weep over him.
For it is written, “Weep over a dead person.” Accompany him until he is buried.
For this is the final commandment that a person can carry out toward his brother. Kiss his body compassionately, saying, “Remember me before the Lord.”
My son, make every effort to observe the things I have written for you.
For they are all building blocks of the monastic life.
Keep death close to you day and night.
For you know that I—the person you know, who is speaking with you—have never thought to myself:
While one of my feet is inside the threshold, “I will live until I get beyond the threshold of the door.”
You too, my son, always place all your thoughts before God, and all these thoughts of weakness will not lead you astray.
Always reflect on the punishments.
Be like God while you are in your dwelling.
If a brother comes to you, rejoice with him.
Greet him.
Pour water over his feet, so that you do not forget yourself.
Let him pray, and sit down.
Kiss his hands and his feet.
Do not ask him, “Where are you coming from?”
For it is written, “Through this some have welcomed angels without knowing it.”
Believe that he has come to you as God.
If he is greater than you, say to him repeatedly, “Grace has come to me, for I have seen you, my lord.”
Set out your table and eat with him. Even if you are bound by a fast, release yourself from it.
For it is written, my son, “I have become all things with everyone.” When he is about to leave,
escort him out, rejoicing with him and being cheerful.
Do all you can to have him bless you three times, so that the blessing of the angel who walks with him may come upon you.
As for the faith of the catholic church, do not let them draw you back from it, nor withdraw from it yourself.
We believe in one God, the Father Almighty, and his only-begotten Son, Jesus Christ our Lord, through whom everything came into being,
and in the Holy Spirit. This is the blessed Trinity.
This is the fullness of the Godhead.
He is God in God.
He is light from light.
He is Lord from Lord.
He is begotten, not created.
He was born as a human being.
He is not a created being, but God, born through the holy Virgin Mary, the Mother of God.
He took a human body for our sake, so that the earth could bear him.
He appointed preachers for himself, namely his holy apostles, as it is written: “Their voice has gone out over the whole earth.”
They crucified him and pierced him with a spear, and our salvation flowed out:
water and blood, which are baptism and the precious blood.
For if you are not baptized, you do not receive the blood.
You too, my son, keep this faith, and the God of peace will be with you. He will save you and deliver you, and you will be at ease all your days.
Farewell in the Lord, my beloved son in the Lord.
Remember me too, my beloved in the Lord, through Jesus our Lord, to whom belong glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.
